analysis.title: Problems Yes, Crisis No - That Comes Later
key_insights: The equity market and the economy are not in crisis, but the economy is heading toward a collision of competing aims: domestic capital demand, a Fed leaning against deficit-driven inflation, and the Administration's policy of redirecting production to the US.

AI is an unmeasurable supply force that makes transactions cheaper. What it makes cheaper disappears from GDP, and people remain the scarce resource. Indeed data cited: about 66% of job postings that mention AI ask people to use AI, not create it.
AI hardware is imported and data plant construction is barely visible in the data. The author argues the economic gain comes from what the plants produce, not from construction.
AI-related multiple expansion is expected to rest increasingly with industries that benefit from adoption over time, many of which have been margin challenged for decades.

The author puts the probability of a 50bp Fed hike in December at closer to 50/50, not just above 10%, and has said so since the October FOMC. If the FOMC does not go 50 while the data run continues, Warsh reverts to his pre-Jackson Hole stance.

Rolling 60-day correlations show the current weakness is narrow. Info technology correlation with the S&P 500 is near one, while consumer staples and financials correlations have been shrinking since April. This pattern is read as a bull-market separation of performance, not a bear market.

In the 2008-09 bear market, the same sectors were highly correlated with the market going in and during the downturn, apart from a brief move into staples. In the dot-com crash, correlations moved toward one as the bear market took hold.

The dot-com analogy is rejected: most dot-com firms had no earnings, and the real funds rate was 4.8% versus 0.9% today. After the dot-com crash the equity market did not bottom until October 2002 and unemployment peaked in June 2003, because the wealth loss was real.
Household equity exposure has risen since then, and even the bottom 50% of net worth has about a 15% tie to equities. Wealth loss is therefore not meaningless for the US economy.

Credit spreads show no crisis. HY technology spreads have widened but have been wider before, and consumer staples HY spreads have collapsed. HY OAS versus investment grade shows no great concern about debt quality.

The deficit is 6.4% of GDP on a rolling 12-month basis and the primary deficit is 3.2% of GDP. Since 1980 a primary deficit this size has aligned with a slowing economy. Interest expense is 3.2% of GDP, the highest since 1992, when the 5Y yield was 6.5% versus 4.9% now.

Debt service costs worsen next year as the primary deficit expands and the Fed hikes while Treasury finances at the short end of the curve. The Fed is no longer creating deposits through QE, so the deficit absorbs domestic savings.

The AI-driven deflation that Warsh is counting on is unlikely, since it does not yet reach the major sources of inflation, beginning with rent. Near-term topline inflation relief is possible if the war with Iran winds down, but base inflation will become more evident through 2027.
Historically the Fed resets policy after about a 10% equity decline. Current weakness is a revaluation of AI profit growth and does not call for a Fed rescue.

The author expects a major bear market eventually, triggered when private capital demand, the rising deficit, inflation and Fed policy strain the economy and flip equities, which have traded up against a 100-year bull trend line. The 10Y is forecast to reach 6% next year and top at 8%. November employment will signal the December move.

tension_points.bull_case: Weakness is narrow: staples and financials correlations to the S&P 500 have fallen since April, credit spreads show no crisis, and the real funds rate is 0.9% versus 4.8% at the dot-com peak.
tension_points.bear_case: Deficit at 6.4% of GDP, interest expense at 3.2% of GDP, a Fed hiking into 2027 and equities against a 100-year trend line will eventually flip the market and bring a major bear market.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Correlations across sectors moving toward one, or an equity decline of about 10% that forces a Fed policy reset.
